title: Rethinking Convergence in MoE Training: The Role of Routing Sparsity
claim: Training loss gap to dense routing shrinks as more experts are activated, consistently across datasets, supporting that larger K speeds convergence.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared legend style, one line plot per dataset
description: Three side-by-side line plots, one each for Alpaca, Dolly and GSM8K. The x-axis is training iterations T from 0 to 10000. The y-axis is Loss Gap, the absolute difference between sparse-routing loss and dense-routing loss. Each panel has five colored curves with markers, labeled Top-1 (blue circle), Top-2 (orange square), Top-4 (green triangle), Top-8 (red inverted triangle) and Top-12 (purple diamond). Top-1 stays near zero. Top-2 climbs highest, to about 0.8 on Alpaca, 1.05 on Dolly and 0.4 on GSM8K. The higher-K curves plateau at lower gaps. On GSM8K, Top-4 and Top-8 rise and then decline. A legend sits in the upper left of each panel, and light gridlines run behind the curves.
caption: Loss gap vs T on Alpaca, Dolly, and GSM8K under different K, where the loss gap is the absolute difference between the loss values of sparse routing and dense routing.
abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training, sparse routing, i.e., activating only the top-$K$ experts per token, is essential for balancing convergence speed and computational cost. However, existing works typically choose $K$ empirically, without theoretical guidance. To address this gap, we characterize the convergence behavior of MoE training using stochastic optimization theory. Specifically, we derive a convergence upper bound of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1+M/K}{\sqrt{T}}\right)$, where $T$ is the number of training iterations and $M$ is the total number of experts per MoE layer. This result guarantees convergence and shows that increasing $K$ can accelerate training. By further fixing the total computational budget $R$ (in FLOPs), we obtain a refined bound of $\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{K}{R}} + \frac{M}{\sqrt{K R}}\right)$, which is convex in $K$ and implies the existence of an optimal $K^{*}\in[1,M]$ that achieves the best convergence performance. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical analysis under diverse settings.
